What is Leonardo AI useful for?

Leonardo AI provides creative tools for generating images, using references to guide visual choices and editing artwork. You can use those tools together in a sequence. Generate a few distinct ideas, choose one that fits the brief, then refine the composition or details that need work. Keep the decisions that the client approves so you can make related images without starting from a blank prompt each time.

Generated concepts can be useful during planning. A concept may show an atmosphere, layout or illustration style before the final production begins. If the finished job requires an exact product, label or existing person, use the approved source and review the result closely. The stronger the requirement for exact details, the more important it is to check the final image against those references.

Write a brief around the intended placement

Imagine a freelancer is preparing a hero image for a travel newsletter. The editor wants a quiet mountain scene with space for a headline. Begin by describing the main subject, composition, time of day and color direction. Ask for a wide frame with the most detailed part of the scene away from the planned text. The result should work as a newsletter header as well as an attractive picture by itself.

Plan the dimensions before generating a large set. A wide layout can place a subject at one side, while a square preview may need it closer to the center. If the image will be cropped by an app, keep important elements inside the area that remains visible. Write down the one detail the reader should notice first. This makes it easier to choose between two appealing images.

Compare ideas that make different decisions

Try a small set of versions that explore useful alternatives. One could show the mountain from a distance, another could give the reader a closer view of a cabin and a third could focus on a path through the scene. Each changes what the audience notices. Select the version that fits the story and leaves room for the intended text. If all the drafts make the same composition choice, revise the brief rather than requesting more of the same.

Keep a record of the prompts and references for selected drafts. Name the versions so a reviewer knows which direction they represent. A brief note about why an image worked is more useful than a folder full of unlabelled pictures. It helps you reproduce the important parts of the style later, even if the next image uses a different subject.

Use image guidance to preserve useful traits

A reference can help communicate a visual idea that would take several sentences to describe. It may show a framing choice, a color palette or the relationship between objects. Decide which part of the reference matters. If you want its composition, explain what the subject should look like separately. If you want its mood, describe which parts of the final scene should change.

Use references you are allowed to share and use. For client work, check whether the images are approved for the tool and the project. If a brand has a fixed logo or product photo, preserve the official artwork separately so you can apply it accurately during final design. Check each result for changes to labels, shapes and product details before showing it as an example of the real offer.

Keep a series consistent without repeating the same image

For the newsletter example, several future issues could share the same color direction and balanced placement. Save a short style reference with the approved look. Describe how much space the headline needs, what level of detail suits the publication and which colors should remain dominant. Then adapt the subject and framing to the story in each issue.

Review the images together. Differences in lighting and contrast may become clearer when several headers appear side by side. Adjust the ones that drift away from the chosen direction. If the same reference keeps producing nearly identical scenes, specify a new camera angle or a different subject arrangement while preserving the approved visual choices.

Refine the image on the canvas

Canvas editing is useful when a strong image needs a targeted change. You may need extra space around the subject or a cleaner part of the background. Identify the specific area to change and the elements that should remain. Work on a copy so you can return to the accepted version if the edit affects more of the picture than you intended.

Review the edge of the changed area. Shadows, repeated patterns and changes in light can reveal where a revision was made. If the output adds a new object or changes part of the subject, adjust the instruction or choose another edit. For a design with precise typography, add the final text in a layout editor where you can control spacing, size and spelling.

Check details before export

Zoom in on important parts of the image. Review hands, text, reflections, repeated objects and edges. Then zoom back out to the intended size. A small visual problem may be irrelevant in a background but noticeable in a full-screen image. Prioritize details that affect the meaning and finish of the work.

If the final asset is for a website, export a version that fits the actual placement and stays clear at a practical file size. Keep the larger source and working version. If the client needs print or another high-resolution output, review the dimensions and the print provider’s requirements before promising a particular result.

Make AI artwork work with other design tools

For a complete layout, consider using a separate design editor for text, logo placement and exact dimensions. For quick branded layouts, compare Canva. For more detailed editing and layered files, see Adobe Creative Cloud. A generated illustration can be a useful ingredient in a design while the editor helps you prepare the final composition.

For projects that need stock photography or editable vectors, explore Freepik and Vecteezy. For a consistent set of interface icons, review IconScout. If you are developing a wider campaign brief, compare Designs.ai. Choose resources according to what the final project actually needs.

Plan client approval and usage rights

Agree on the types of material you can use before starting. A client may want concepts for internal review or may need visuals ready for publication. Explain which assets are provided by the client and which are generated. Keep approved versions and relevant source information in the project folder. If a use depends on exclusive rights, precise brand controls or particular terms, confirm those requirements before accepting the final design.

Avoid using sensitive client material for a test without the appropriate permission. Start with an approved public reference or a simple sample. If a project needs private generations, team controls or a particular account arrangement, confirm the relevant features and terms. Keep the source image and final exports organized separately from the drafts.

List the visual jobs you expect to do during the access period. If you regularly need new design concepts or backgrounds, compare the time spent creating, selecting and refining images with your current workflow. For a product catalog that needs exact photos, a photo editor may handle more of the work. Try a representative brief and count the time required to reach the final usable image.

Keep the test small enough to review thoroughly. Select one image that needs consistent style and one that needs a targeted edit. Check whether you can reproduce the approved direction and whether the final file works on the actual page. The practical value comes from finishing images you can publish, including the time needed to review and prepare them.

Frequently asked questions

Can I use Leonardo AI for social graphics?

It can help create visual concepts and artwork for social posts. Use a layout editor to add precise text and any official brand elements. Preview the result on a phone and check whether the main subject remains visible after the platform crop. Review the terms for the intended use and keep the accepted version for future formats.

What is image guidance for?

Image guidance helps communicate the visual traits you want to carry into a new result. A reference can provide a framing example or show the mood you want. Describe what should stay and what should change. Review the result for unwanted changes before reusing it in a series or making it part of a client delivery.

Can I change part of an image?

Use a copy of the accepted image and identify the area to refine. A targeted edit can help change a distracting detail or extend the composition. Compare the result with the original around the edited area. If the revision affects important parts of the subject, keep the better version and adjust the instruction before trying again.

Run a simple prompt test before building a series

Write one brief and choose one starting setup. Keep a copy of the first result. For the next test, change only the framing instruction, such as switching from a wide establishing scene to a close view of the subject. Compare how that change affects the composition. If you change the style, subject and camera angle together, it becomes harder to tell which instruction improved the result.

Try a second test around color. Use the same subject and composition, then describe a specific set of colors that supports the brand. A warm cream and blue accent might work for a newsletter, while a muted palette could suit a documentary image. Review the generated asset against the approved colors. Apply exact brand colors to text, borders and backgrounds in the final layout when precision matters.

Prepare a version for mobile review

Place the image into a rough version of the real page before the design is approved. Check both the wide view and the mobile crop. Read the heading over the image and make sure the background does not hide it. If you need a different crop, prepare a mobile version rather than squeezing the whole image into a narrow frame. Keep the two versions in the same folder with clear names. That way a colleague can apply the right file without guessing from a thumbnail.

The review can also reveal an image that works better without text. In that case, move the heading into a separate page element and keep the artwork focused on its subject.
